full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. These two Civil Appeals, by leave, are directed against the judgment and order dated 15.06.2014, passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 5210 of 2013, filed by the Delta Spinner and others (the present respondents), heard along with Writ Petition No. 93)5 of 2013, making both the Rules Nisi absolute and thereby directing the Letter of Credit (LC) issuing banks (Sonali Bank and Krishi Bank) as well as the Bangladesh Bank "to ensure reimbursement of the said bills of the writ petitioners within a period of two months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment". However, in respect of writ petitioners' claim of interests the High Court Division did not issue any direction upon the respondents as the claims need determination of facts upon adducing evidences, but the writ petitioners were given liberty to realize the same 4 through proper forum in accordance with law. 

 2. On the other hand Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2971 of 2015 is directed against the judgment and order dated 07.01.2015 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 10370 of 2013, filed by Zaheen Spinning Limited and others, making the Rule Nisi absolute with direction upon the writ respondents No. 2 and 3 to make payment against the accepted bills along with overdue interests under the concerned Letters of Credit(LC) within 60 days from the date of receipt of the judgment and order. 

 4. That the present respondent No.1, in both the appeals and in the civil petition moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition Nos. 5210 of 2013, 9305 of 2013 and 10370 of 2013 respectively, stating, inter alia, that they are engaged in the business of manufacturing and supplying yarn being registered with the Board of Investment (BOI) and Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA). In course of their respective businesses, the writ petitioners received some back to back Letters of Credit (in short "BBL/Cs"), in 2011, issued by Sonali Bank, Bangladesh Krishi Bank etc. at the instance of the purchaser, Hall Mark Fashion Limited, for supply of yarn to the said purchaser. The expiry dates of the said LCs in two appeals were 20.08.2011, 25.09.2011 and on different dates from January to June 2012 in the civil petition stipulating that the negotiating bank, namely, the Agrani Bank Limited, Amin Court Branch, Dhaka, i.e. writ respondent No. 4 (in Writ Petition Nos. 5210 of 2013 and 9305 of 2013) and respondent Nos. 4 to 7 (in Writ Petition No. 10370 of 2013) would get the payment against the said L/Cs after twenty days on maturity and that the payment would only be due upon fulfillment of the conditions incorporated in the said L/Cs as well as in the letter of acceptance of the said L/Cs by the L/C issuing bank. Upon receipt of the said L/Cs, after endorsement by the negotiating bank, the writ-petitioners manufactured the "yarn" and supplied the same upon fulfilling the terms and conditions mentioned in the said L/Cs and, accordingly, submitted the delivery documents, such as, deli, (Tery challans, Mushak-11 forms etc., before the negotiating bank. Whereupon the negotiating hank. having found no discrepancy in the said documents and rather the same being in compliance with the terms of the said L/Cs, issued forwarding letters to the L/C issuing banks indicating that the said supply of yarns was made by the writ petitioners as against the said L/Cs. Upon receipt of the said supply by the purchasers, Hall Mark Fashion Limited, the negotiating bank made payments against the said bills to the writ petitioners and, accordingly, forwarded the said bills to the L/C issuing banks through official channel for reimbursement. But, even after the expiry of the maturity dates, as stipulated in the said L/Cs, the L/C issuing Banks having not paid or reimbursed the said L/C amounts, the negotiating bank issued several letters addressing the L/C issuing Bank for taking necessary steps to reimburse the said amounts upon honouring the said bills. But L/C issuing Banks did not pay any heed to the same. Under such circumstances the negotiating bank started taking steps for realizing the said amounts from the writ petitioners by issuing letters stating that since the L/C issuing bank did not honour the said bills the writ-petitioner was liable to pay the same. It is further stated that since the negotiating bank has taken steps for realization of the said amounts from the writ petitioner for no fault on their part but for the fault of the L/C issuing banks in honoring the said L/Cs in accordance with law, the writ-petitioners are at the high risk of being treated as defaulting-borrowers and classified in the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) report, published by the Bangladesh Bank thereby depriving the writ petitioners from getting any credit facility from any bank or financial institution in future. Consequent to such step/ attempts of the negotiating bank the business of the writ-petitioners are facing serious impacts only because of the default of the L/C issuing bank. Thus the writ-petitioners moved the High Court Division in the aforementioned writ petitions challenging the inaction of the L/C issuing banks in paying the outstanding export bills of the writ petitioners along with the interest as per terms of the Letters of Credit for non-payment of the same on the date of maturity. Moreover, for such inaction, overdue interest of the Proforma Respondent No. 4 against the Letters of Credit are being increased as shown in different annexures which do not fall under the cause of fraud of the writ petitioners unless it is found by investigation, specially, conducted by the Anti-Corruption Commission. Thus, the writ petitioners also prayed for direction upon the writ respondents Nos. 1, 2 and 3 to take necessary steps for payment of the said outstanding export bills as stated above along with 16% interest for delay and other overdue charges and thereby obtained Rules Nisi. 

 9. Under similar facts and circumstances Zaheen Spinning Limited moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 10370 of 2013 challenging similar inaction of Sonali Bank Ltd. and Bangladesh Bank along with other proforma respondents and obtained Rule Nisi. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record also made the said Rule Nisi absolute by judgment and order dated 07.01.2015 directing the writ respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to make payment against the accepted bills along with overdue interest under the letters of credit within 60 days from the date of receipt of the judgment and order. Challenging the same, writ respondent Nos. 2 and 3 Sonali Bank Ltd. filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2971 of 2015 before this Division for redress. 

 13. Mr. M.A. Sobhan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner (Sonali Bank), in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2971 of 2015 submits that since the writ petition involved a complicated disputed question of fact the same requires investigation into facts and should be determined upon taking evidence. Thus, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law. 

 16. Mr. N.K. Saha, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2971 of 2015 supported the impugned judgment and order passed in Writ Petition No. 10370 of 2013. 

 18. From the record it appears that for the purpose of exporting certain goods the appellant-Sonali Bank Limited, Hotel Sheraton Branch, Dhaka, issued Back to Back Letters of Credit in 2011 at the instance of Hall Mark Fashions Limited for supplying of yarn by the writ petitioner company to the purchaser Hall Mark Fashion Limited fixing expiry dates of those letters of credit on various dates from August 2011 to June, 2012 wherein Agrani Bank was the negotiating Bank in respect of two civil appeals and pro forma respondents Nos. 4 to 7 ( In Writ Petition No. 10370 of 2013), namely, Mutual Trust Bank Limited, National Credit and Commerce Bank Limited, Bank Asia Limited and BRAC Bank Limited was the negotiating Banks in respect of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2971 of 2015. It was contemplated in the letters of credit that the negotiating banks would get the payment against the said letters of credit after twenty days on maturity of the same whereupon payment would only be due upon fulfillment of the conditions incorporated in the said letters of credit as well as in the letters of acceptance by L/C issuing bank. It is claimed by the writ petitioner-respondent that the negotiating banks having found no discrepancy in the documents, regarding delivery of the goods, submitted by the writ petitioners respondent and the same being found to be in compliance with the terms of letters of credit, issued the forwarding letters to the L/C issuing Banks indicating that the supply of yarn was made against the said letters of credit which the purchaser, (Hall Mark Fashions Limited) has received and as such, the negotiating banks made payment against the said bills to the writ petitioner and forwarded the same to the L/C issuing bank for re-imbursement. But it is alleged that after the expiry of maturity dates of those letters of credit the L/C issuing bank did not reimburse the amount even after several requests made by the negotiating banks. Having failed to get reimbursement of the bills the negotiating banks issued letters upon the writ petitioner-respondent to make necessary arrangement against the amount already paid by the negotiating banks. So it is clear that the dispute arose as to non reimbursement of the L/C amount by the L/C issuing bank against the said bills to the negotiating banks and as such, the negotiating banks is to get the reimbursement of the same from the L/C issuing Bank. But admittedly the negotiating Banks did not come forward for redress. The writ petitioner being a third party to the agreement has come for-ward on the plea that unless the L/C issuing bank reimbursed the money the negotiating banks would realize the same from the writ petitioner. 

 19. It is apparent from the letters of credit that though the writ petitioners claimed that the letters of credit have been opened under the international trade but from the record it appears that there is no element of international trade in the L/Cs as the manufacturer is a local company and the recipient of the manufactured goods is also a local company and there is no indication in the letters of credit that the goods were to be exported out of Bangladesh. Therefore, the letters of credit cannot be, under any circumstances, treated as international trade or transaction. Moreover, the writ petitioner did not annex/produce the main letters of credit against which the back to back letters of credit have been opened and also to prove that the same are international transactions. Under the banking law, back to back L/C can be opened only against an international L/C which is generally termed as Master/ Mother L/C and the number of the said mother L/C is required to be incorporated in the back to back L/C. This is required to prove that the transaction is an international transaction. In the absence of such material on record, the letters of credit can purely be termed as commercial transaction by the local bank wherein the writ petitioner is not a party. Apart from this, from the record it appears that no document has been produced by the writ petitioner respondent to prove that pursuant to the manufacture of the goods, which is the subject matter of letters of credit, no export bill/bills relating to export has been produced to prove that under some foreign letters of credit the order was placed and the goods were manufactured and supplied. For the purpose of smooth running of international trade and commerce the International Chamber of Commerce for Documentary Credit has introduced Uniform Customs and Practice (UCP)-600 with effect on 1st of July, 2007. Thereunder the International Chamber of Commerce authorized the ICC Commission on Banking Technique and Practice (Banking Commission) to follow the guideline in the international commercial arena for the purpose of dealing with such documentary credits. It appears from Article 4 of the said UCP-600 that a beneficiary can in no case avail the contractual relationships existing between the banks or between the applicant and the issuing bank. An issuing bank should discourage any attempt by the applicant to include, as an integral part of the credit, copies of the underlying contract, proforma invoice and the like'. In Article 5 it has been contemplated that 'banks deal with documents and not with goods, services or performance to which the documents may relate. In Article 9 it has been stated that 'before reimbursement of the amount the advising bank has to be satisfied itself as to the apparent authenticity of the credit, and that the advice accurately reflects the terms and conditions of the credit. It must inform the beneficiary or the second advising bank that it has not been able to satisfy itself as to the apparent authenticity of the letter of credit the amendment or the advice'. The main purpose of UCP-600 is to bring system and regularizes the proper transaction in accordance with law which is generally followed by all concerns in the commercial transaction. From the record it appears that pursuant to a good number of similar type of transactions along with the present transaction suspicions have arisen in respect of all such transactions, between a company, namely, Hall Mark Group wherein Sonali Bank Limited is related and party to such suspicious transactions. On the basis of such suspicion the L/C issuing bank subsequently held investigation of its own and found major discrepancies in the sup-ply of the goods under the concerned letters of credit. On the other hand the Anti-Corruption Commission also held investigation and found serious discrepancies in all the transactions of Hall Mark Group with Sonali Bank Limited, Hotel Sheraton Branch, and as such lodged two First Information Reports (FIR) against the persons involved in such transactions and thereby misappropriating huge amount of money on placing false and fabricated bills. As a result several civil and criminal cases have been initiated against Hall Mark Group, its Chairman and Managing Director including some of its officials as well as the writ petitioners. Pursuant to the investigation held by the L/C issuing Bank, it itself found major discrepancies in the papers of the goods under the concerned letters of credit for which the L/C issuing bank withheld/withdrew the reimbursed money to the negotiating banks. The question of discrepancy in the bills and the allegations of misappropriation of fund from the state owned bank are all questions of fact to be determined by a competent Court of law upon taking evidence. When the allegation and the documents filed by the writ petitioner are disputed by the respondents by swearing affidavit and pointing out the discrepancy, the judicial review in that respect is not at all available. The Court in such case generally refrains from interfering with the same. As the judicial review itself is a summary proceeding the High Court Division can adjudicate a case simply on the admitted facts and documents otherwise it cannot interfere with any case. But whenever the facts or documents are disputed by other side on cogent ground the High Court Division cannot exercise its power under article 102 of the Constitution in a summary proceeding and thereby pass order in favour of the writ petitioner. Herein in this case the L/C issuing bank as well as the Bangladesh Bank have repeatedly pointed out that delivery documents submitted by the writ petitioner are false and as such, the writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked until and unless the documents are declared to be genuine by competent Court.
